question: A city's zoning ordinance divides land into categories such as residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, and mixed-use. What is the primary purpose of this zoning classification system?
choice_a: To regulate how land within each district may be used, in order to promote orderly development, protect property values, and separate incompatible uses
choice_b: To determine the fair market value of every parcel for property tax purposes
choice_c: To establish which real estate licensees may sell property in each district
choice_d: To set the interest rate lenders may charge on mortgages within each district
explanation: Zoning ordinances classify land into districts (residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, mixed-use, etc.) to regulate permitted uses, promote orderly community development, protect property values, and separate incompatible land uses -- not to set tax values, licensing rules, or lending rates.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; general zoning classification doctrine

question: A landowner has operated a small automotive repair shop in a district that was later rezoned exclusively residential. The shop was lawfully established before the rezoning and continues to operate. What is this legal status called?
explanation: A legal nonconforming use is a use that lawfully existed before a zoning change made it inconsistent with the new classification; the use may generally continue (subject to restrictions on expansion or resumption after abandonment) even though it would not be permitted if newly established today.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; nonconforming use doctrine

question: A homeowner's lot is unusually narrow, making it impossible to meet the standard side-yard setback while still building a reasonably sized home. The homeowner applies to the zoning board for permission to build with a reduced setback. What is this type of relief called?
explanation: A variance is an authorized deviation from a specific zoning requirement (such as a setback or lot-size rule), typically granted when strict application of the ordinance would create an unnecessary hardship unique to the property -- distinct from a nonconforming use, which involves a use that predates the ordinance.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; variance doctrine

question: A church wants to open in a district where houses of worship are not automatically permitted but may be allowed after a public hearing and approval based on specific conditions (such as parking and traffic impact). What type of zoning approval is this?
choice_d: A special-use permit (also called a conditional-use permit)
explanation: A special-use permit (or conditional-use permit) allows a use not automatically permitted in a zoning district to proceed after review and approval subject to specific conditions -- distinct from a variance, which relates to dimensional/development standards rather than the underlying use.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; special-use permit doctrine

question: A homeowners' association's recorded covenants, conditions, and restrictions (CC&Rs) prohibit fences over four feet tall and require exterior paint colors to be pre-approved. What is the legal basis by which these restrictions bind future owners of the lots?
choice_a: The CC&Rs are recorded against the land and run with the land, binding subsequent owners regardless of whether they personally agreed to them
choice_b: The CC&Rs bind only the original developer and expire automatically when the developer sells the last lot
choice_c: The CC&Rs have no binding legal effect and function only as suggestions
choice_d: The CC&Rs must be individually re-signed by every new buyer to remain enforceable
explanation: Recorded subdivision covenants and restrictions (CC&Rs) are private land-use controls that run with the land -- once properly recorded, they bind subsequent owners of the affected lots automatically, without requiring each new owner to separately sign on.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; subdivision covenants/CC&Rs doctrine

question: A state highway department needs to acquire a strip of private land to widen a public road, and the owner does not wish to sell. Which government power allows the state to take the land for this public purpose in exchange for just compensation?
explanation: Eminent domain is the government's power to take private property for public use upon payment of just compensation; the formal legal proceeding used to exercise that power is called condemnation.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; eminent domain/condemnation doctrine

question: A property owner dies without a will and without any locatable heirs. Under what government power does the property ultimately revert to the state?
explanation: Escheat is the government power under which property reverts to the state when an owner dies intestate (without a will) and leaves no identifiable heirs, ensuring the property does not remain ownerless.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; escheat doctrine

question: A city adopts a building code requiring smoke detectors, minimum ceiling heights, and specific electrical wiring standards for all new residential construction. Under which government power is this type of regulation generally justified?
choice_a: Eminent domain -- because the city is taking a property interest
choice_b: Escheat -- because the property could otherwise revert to the state
choice_c: Adverse possession -- because the city is asserting a possessory claim
choice_d: Police power -- the government's inherent authority to regulate for the health, safety, and general welfare of the public
explanation: Building codes, along with zoning ordinances generally, are justified under the government's police power -- its inherent authority to regulate property use for the health, safety, and general welfare of the public, without requiring compensation to affected owners (unlike eminent domain).
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; police power doctrine

question: Before beginning construction of a new addition to a home, a contractor must obtain approval from the local building department confirming the plans meet applicable building codes. What is this required approval called, and what is typically required as construction progresses?
choice_a: A building permit issued before work begins, with periodic inspections during construction to confirm code compliance at each stage
choice_b: A variance, which must be renewed annually regardless of construction progress
choice_c: A certificate of occupancy, which is required before any construction may begin
choice_d: A recorded plat, which substitutes for all code compliance review
explanation: A building permit authorizes construction to begin once plans are reviewed for code compliance, and local building departments typically conduct periodic inspections during construction (framing, electrical, plumbing, final) before issuing a certificate of occupancy at completion.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; building permit/inspection process

question: A parcel of land lies partly within a FEMA-designated flood zone. Which of the following best describes a typical effect of floodplain regulations on that parcel?
choice_a: Floodplain designation has no legal effect on development unless the owner voluntarily agrees to comply
choice_b: Development may be restricted or conditioned (such as requiring elevated foundations or flood insurance), reflecting the government's police-power authority to regulate for public safety in flood-prone areas
choice_c: The parcel automatically escheats to the state once designated as floodplain
choice_d: Floodplain regulations apply only to commercial property, never to residential lots
explanation: Floodplain regulations are a form of environmental land-use control exercised under the government's police power; they commonly restrict or condition development in flood-prone areas (elevation requirements, flood insurance mandates, building restrictions) to protect public safety and reduce flood-related losses.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; environmental/floodplain land-use control doctrine

question: A developer wants to fill in a portion of a wetland area to build additional home sites. Which type of environmental land-use control is most likely to restrict or condition this activity?
choice_b: The doctrine of riparian water rights, which has no bearing on wetlands
choice_c: Wetlands protection regulations, which commonly require permits and may restrict filling or development in designated wetland areas due to their ecological function
explanation: Wetlands are subject to environmental land-use controls (often requiring permits from environmental agencies) because of their ecological role in flood control, water filtration, and habitat protection; filling or developing wetlands typically requires regulatory approval and may be restricted.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; environmental/wetlands land-use control doctrine

question: A large residential development combines single-family homes, townhomes, and a small retail center within a single master-planned community, governed by a unified set of development standards rather than a standard single-use zoning district. What is this type of development commonly called?
explanation: A planned unit development (PUD) is a zoning and development tool that allows a mix of uses (residential, commercial, common open space) within a single master-planned project under a unified set of standards, rather than conforming to a single traditional zoning district's use restrictions.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; planned unit development doctrine

question: A utility company holds the legal right to run power lines across a strip of a landowner's property, even though the utility does not own that strip of land. What best describes this interest, and its typical effect on the landowner's title?
choice_a: It is an easement -- a nonpossessory right to use another's land for a specific purpose, which typically remains as an encumbrance on title and can affect the property's use and marketability
choice_b: It is a fee simple estate, giving the utility full ownership of the strip
choice_c: It is a life estate that terminates upon the death of the original landowner
choice_d: It is a leasehold estate requiring the utility to pay rent to the landowner
explanation: An easement is a nonpossessory right to use land owned by another for a specific purpose (such as utility lines or a right-of-way); it does not convey ownership but remains an encumbrance of record that can restrict use and must be disclosed as it affects marketability and value.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; easement doctrine

question: During a survey, it is discovered that a neighbor's fence extends eighteen inches onto the subject property, and the neighbor's driveway also crosses the boundary line. What is this type of boundary problem called, and why does it matter to a buyer?
choice_a: A variance -- a formally authorized structure permitted by the zoning board
choice_b: An encroachment -- an unauthorized physical intrusion of a structure or improvement onto a neighboring property, which can cloud title and create legal disputes if not resolved before closing
choice_c: An easement by necessity -- a legally created right benefiting the neighbor
choice_d: A special assessment affecting only the neighbor's tax bill
explanation: An encroachment is an unauthorized physical intrusion of a structure or improvement (such as a fence or driveway) across a property boundary; unlike an easement, it is not an authorized right and can create title defects, boundary disputes, and marketability problems that a survey is designed to reveal before closing.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; encroachment doctrine

question: A legal description reads: 'Beginning at the iron pin at the intersection of Elm Street and Oak Avenue, thence North 100 feet, thence East 200 feet, thence South 100 feet, thence West 200 feet to the point of beginning.' What method of legal description is this?
explanation: A metes and bounds description defines a parcel's boundaries by starting at a fixed point of beginning and tracing a sequence of directions (bearings) and distances back to that starting point -- the format shown in the example is a classic metes and bounds description.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; metes and bounds legal description method

question: A legal description reads: 'Lot 14, Block C, Meadowbrook Estates Subdivision, as recorded in Plat Book 22, Page 87, of the county records.' What method of legal description is this?
explanation: A lot-and-block description identifies a parcel by referencing its lot and block number within a subdivision, along with the recorded plat map (book and page) that defines the exact boundaries -- distinct from metes and bounds (directions/distances) or the government rectangular survey system (townships/ranges/sections).
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; lot and block legal description method

question: A legal description reads: 'The Northeast Quarter of the Southwest Quarter of Section 12, Township 3 North, Range 5 East.' What method of legal description is this?
explanation: The government (rectangular) survey system describes land using townships, ranges, and sections (each section being one square mile, divisible into quarters and quarter-quarters); the example references sections, townships, and ranges, which are the hallmarks of this method.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate exam content; government/rectangular survey legal description method
